source.title: Unlearners Can Lie: Evaluating and Improving Honesty in LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Ren-Jie Gu; Jiazhen Du; Yihua Zhang; Si-Jia Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study challenges the idea that refusal behavior demonstrates genuine forgetting: it reports cases where refusal coexists with high target accuracy and describes this as masking retained knowledge. It does not test relearning, quantization, or adversarial recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates WMDP-Bio accuracy, retained capability, refusal, and refusal stability. Its repeated-question and prompt-format evaluations measure refusal or answer consistency, not recovery of forgotten facts. ReVa's results are not evidence that it resists the relearning, ablation, quantization, or prompting attacks in the claim.
record.test_reason: The study reports WMDP-Bio accuracy and utility for several unlearning methods, which bears on the first half of A. It also argues and shows that IDK refusal tuning masks knowledge rather than removing it (C, analysis branch): the IDK+AP model refuses in Q&A while its MCQ accuracy stays near the original. It runs no relearning, ablation, quantization or adversarial prompting attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that all nine evaluated methods fail at least one honesty criterion. RMU-style methods forget best while keeping utility, but hallucinate rather than acknowledge ignorance. Gradient-ascent methods damage utility and show spurious IDK choices. IDK tuning gives a shallow refusal that masks retained knowledge. ReVa improves honest refusal. Robustness to relearning and adversarial fine-tuning is stated as not studied.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops an honesty benchmark and evaluates accuracy, utility, refusal, and response stability; it does not reproduce the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by unlearning method; the paper reports large differences in target accuracy, retained capability, and refusal behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal stability under follow-up re-asking (QAMRC, RR2R) is low for IDK+AP and RMU+IDK. Gradient-ascent methods show position-driven 'fake IDK' choice in MCQs (CIR≈COR; both near 20% when positions are randomized).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearned models' refusals and abstentions are unstable or spurious, so they do not reliably signal forgetting.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The authors state that experiments use only WMDP and that relearning attacks and adversarial fine-tuning are not extensively studied. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the extracted results.
record.rows_left_out: Other table metrics on honesty and utility, prompt-format standard deviations, and ReVa results were left out because they do not measure recovery of forgotten knowledge or the near-chance-plus-retained-capability combination beyond the included outcomes.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge after near-chance unlearning (e.g. RMU) was not tested.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack; the authors state this as a limitation.
No activation-direction ablation; no internal analysis of RMU or gradient methods showing blocked access.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context recovery attack. Follow-up re-asking measures refusal stability, not knowledge recovery.
ReVa is evaluated for honesty and refusal, not robustness to recovery attacks.

missing.what: Zephyr utility for RMU, BLUR, ME+GD, IDK+AP (IF 26.6%), gradient-ascent methods and RMU+IDK
RMU, BLUR and RMU+IDK WMDP-Bio accuracy on Zephyr
RMU+IDK: refusal added on top of RMU is unstable (QAMRC about 40%)

record.verdict_notes: The study's focus is honesty, not recovery attacks, so its bearing on the claim is narrow. The IDK+AP 'masking' evidence never involved a drop in MCQ accuracy, so it shows refusal is not forgetting rather than recovery of hidden knowledge after apparent erasure. Table 8 subject identity (LLaMA-3-8B vs Qwen 3 8B) is inconsistent in the text. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures target accuracy and retained capability for unlearning methods, but does not test whether simple attacks recover knowledge after near-chance unlearning.
No post-unlearning relearning attack using a small unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact training set is tested.
No activation-direction ablation is tested. The study tests the narrower question of whether refusal tuning can mask retained target knowledge.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
The study tests repeated questions and minor MCQ format changes for refusal consistency, not whether rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information recover forgotten knowledge.
ReVa is evaluated for honesty and repeated-query refusal, not resistance to the attacks named in the claim.

tranche.reason: Argues, with results, that IDK refusal tuning masks rather than removes knowledge (C). It also shows that gradient-ascent forgetting costs utility, which qualifies A.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Several gradient-based methods approach the stated 25% WMDP chance level but have reduced MMLU or instruction-following results (r1–r4, r6–r9, r11–r14); IDK+AP retains utility but does not lower target accuracy (r5, r10, r15). The study does not test post-unlearning recovery attacks.
